message.content:
**Answer:**

The United States has produced a wide array of composers who have made significant contributions to music across many styles—from classical and jazz to film scores and popular music. Below is a non‑exhaustive list of some of the most widely recognized American composers, grouped roughly by era and genre. (The “most famous” label is inherently subjective, but these names frequently appear in discussions of influential American composers.)

| Composer | Lifespan | Notable Works / Contributions |
|----------|----------|--------------------------------|
| **John Philip Sousa** | 1854–1932 | “The Stars and Stripes Forever,” “Washington Post March.” Known as the “March King.” |
| **George Gershwin** | 1898–1937 | “Rhapsody in Blue,” “An American in Paris,” “Porgy and Bess.” Blended classical and jazz idioms. |
| **Aaron Copland** | 1900–1990 | “Appalachian Spring,” “Rodeo,” “Fanfare for the Common Man.” Modernist yet accessible. |
| **Leonard Bernstein** | 1918–1990 | “West Side Story,” “Candide,” “On the Town.” Composer, conductor, educator. |
| **Samuel Barber** | 1910–1981 | “Adagio for Strings,” “Knoxville: Summer of 1915.” Known for lyrical, expressive style. |
| **Philip Glass** | 1937– | Minimalist composer; “Einstein on the Beach,” “Glassworks.” Influential in contemporary classical. |
| **John Williams** | 1942– | Film scores for “Star Wars,” “Indiana Jones,” “Jurassic Park.” One of the most recognizable film composers. |
| **George Gershwin** | 1898–1937 | “Rhapsody in Blue,” “An American in Paris.” |
| **Charles Ives** | 1874–1954 | Experimental works like “The Unanswered Question.” Early modernist. |
